author: Philip K. Dick
card_summary: Jill Herrick is married to Lester, a toxicologist who develops poisons for the military and who treats warmth, metaphor, food and children as forms of imprecision.
page_summary:
Jill Herrick is married to Lester, a toxicologist who develops poisons for the military and who treats warmth, metaphor, food and children as forms of imprecision. He refuses to let her young nephew Gus stay, corrects the boy's name for his kitten, and invites him to the lab to see the animals they use in research. Jill has decided to leave him. Lester goes to Rexor IV, an old dead world, and returns transformed: courteous, delighted by food and weather, playful with Gus, romantic, uninterested in his work — and speaking in a curiously formal, archaic register. Jill's brother Frank, a Clearance lawyer, recognises the pattern. Rexor IV is dying; its inhabitants have for a century migrated by displacing the minds of visitors, and their idea of human speech comes from centuries-old Terran books, which is exactly how they are detected. The real Lester is alive, held in suspension in the Rexorian ruins, and can be recovered — but only if a court accepts that the man in the room is not him, and the only possible evidence is Jill's testimony. Brought to the Clearance Building to give it, she looks at the man holding his coat and ivory-headed cane and says she has noticed no change. She takes his arm and leaves with him. Walking home, she asks his real name; he says she could not pronounce it. She decides she will go on calling him Lester.

**Why it matters.** The title is a sentence with its predicate removed, and the story is the argument for what completes it. Dick sets up a case in which every legal, factual and familial consideration points one way — the man is an impostor, the husband is alive and retrievable, the wife's duty is to say so — and then has the criterion of the human turn out to be conduct rather than identity. What makes it more than a fable is that Jill's choice is not costless or clean: she is choosing an occupier over a victim, and the story lets that stand without softening it.

*The last exchange is a negotiation over a name. He offers her anything she wishes; she asks only to go on using the name of the man he displaced.*

structure.form: continuous short story in four movements, built as a reversal
movements: The marriage as it is: Lester's cruelty rendered entirely through small domestic refusals.
The absence: Jill tells Frank she is leaving; a week of relief.
The return: the transformation catalogued in detail, and Frank's interrogation of it as evidence.
The Clearance Building: the testimony withheld, and the walk home.
structure.point_of_view: third person aligned with Jill, except for one scene at Clearance from which she is absent — which is where the reader is given the official account and its full plausibility.
structure.narrative_device: The evidence of the alien's presence and the evidence of its goodness are the same evidence. Every detail Frank collects as proof of infiltration — the metaphors, the appetite, the pleasure in weather, the kindness to the child — the reader has already registered as improvement.

characters.name: Jill Herrick
characters.note: Given the entire moral weight of the story in a single refusal. Her decision is not argued for; she simply declines to describe what she has seen.

characters.name: Lester Herrick
characters.note: Two occupants of one body. The first develops poisons for the military and is credited with the weapon used against Callisto; the second cannot remember what toxicology is.

characters.name: The Rexorian
characters.note: Never named — it says the sounds cannot be formed. Its archaic diction is the flaw that identifies it, and the flaw is that it learned humanity from old books.

characters.name: Frank
characters.note: Sympathetic, methodical, and entirely on the side of the law. He is the one who works out what has happened, and he is the one his sister defeats.

characters.name: Gus
characters.note: The test case. The first Lester will not have him in the house; the second builds him an otter slide.

characters.name: Director Douglas
characters.note: Explains the mechanism and confirms the real Lester is recoverable — which is what makes Jill's silence cost something.

settings.name: The Herrick house
settings.note: Automated — a stove on a select-list, a robant waiter, conveyor belts from underground storage. Domestic warmth is entirely absent from the machinery and has to be supplied by a person.

settings.name: Rexor IV
settings.note: Old, dry, dying, squeezed to a pulp by wind and sun. Never shown; known only by report.

settings.name: The Federal Clearance Building
settings.note: Where the story's question is put formally and answered by refusal.

motifs: Archaic diction as the tell — the alien is caught by being two hundred years out of date, having learned people from novels
Food and appetite as evidence of a soul; the first Lester wanted intravenous intake made universal
The kitten called a tiger, and the correction of it — the story's whole ethic in one exchange
Testimony withheld: the plot is resolved by something a character declines to say
Naming: she keeps the name and gives up the man

distinctive_terms.label: Scanner
distinctive_terms.note: The desk scanner Lester feeds report tapes through. The word carries a much heavier charge later in Dick, and its appearance here is mechanical rather than thematic — recorded so the concordance does not overstate the link.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Dick called this his favourite of his own stories and, in the strongest statement he made about any of them, his credo.

evidence.source: Author's story note (The Collected Stories of Philip K. Dick)
evidence.quote: To me, this story states my early conclusions as to what is human. I have not really changed my view since I wrote this story, back in the Fifties. It's not what you look like, or what planet you were born on. It's how kind you are. The quality of kindness, to me, distinguishes us from rocks and sticks and metal, and will forever, whatever shape we take, wherever we go, whatever we become. For me , Human Is is my credo. May it be yours. (1976)
evidence.reading: Dick's clearest, most personal statement of the story's thesis, written as a credo rather than analysis: kindness, not origin or substrate, is what constitutes the human.

evidence.quote: My favorite short story of my own is one called "Human Is", and I can't locate a copy of it anywhere
evidence.reading: Stated plainly, and with the wry detail that he could not find a copy. Weighs heavily against the general difficulty of getting Dick to rank his own work.

evidence.quote: For me, "Human Is" is my credo. May it be yours.
evidence.reading: The end of Dick's own note on the story. The preceding sentence in the captured window runs '…and sticks and metal, and will forever, whatever shape we take, wherever we go, whatever we become' — the full passage should be read at the locator before it is quoted at length.

evidence.quote: of all the omissions, "Human Is" stands as most glaring. It must be included.
evidence.reading: Arguing with an editor over a collection's contents. He adds that his entire 'Afterthoughts' statement depends on the story and makes no sense without it.

evidence.quote: I have not really changed my view since I wrote this
evidence.reading: Written decades later. One of the few positions Dick claims never to have revised.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: a woman is married to the very embodiment o…
evidence.reading: Palmer opens his discussion of Dick's family stories with this one, pairing it with 'The Pre-Persons' as stories set in outwardly typical American households.

evidence.author: Christopher Palmer
evidence.quote: "Human Is" is unlikely to annoy anyone
evidence.reading: A pointed comparison: Palmer finds 'The Pre-Persons' offensive and uses this story's inoffensiveness as the foil. A backhanded assessment worth keeping against Dick's own valuation of it as his credo.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.reading: Sutin groups it with 'Impostor', noting that in both the artificial or alien party wins the reader's sympathy over the human pursuers.

contradictions.summary: Dick calls the story his credo; Palmer calls it unlikely to annoy anyone.

claim_a.text: For me, 'Human Is' is my credo.

claim_b.text: 'Human Is' is unlikely to annoy anyone

contradictions.note: Palmer is not disparaging the story so much as using it to measure a more abrasive one. But the gap between an author's credo and a critic's 'inoffensive' is exactly the kind of disagreement worth preserving rather than smoothing.

open_questions: Dick says his 'Afterthoughts' statement depends on this story. Which collection is that, and is the statement in the archive?

The full Dick note quoted by Sutin appears to run several sentences before 'For me, "Human Is" is my credo.' The scripted gather captured only a window; the passage should be read at Sutin l.1447-1453 and transcribed properly.
The first Lester is credited with the copper sulphate weapon used against Callisto. Does any other story in the corpus share that reference?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.
